title: Streaming essentials: chat params & retry strategies - Alder Health intro
summary: Intro demo covering Redwood hosted API streaming behavior, key generation parameters, retries and graceful fallbacks. Discussed latency vs cost tradeoffs, console monitoring, and next steps for a short pilot and security review.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-15 16:00 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (CTO - Alder Health), Sam Torres (Platform Eng), Elena Ruiz (ML Eng)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, I'm the AE on the account, and I have Liam here from the SE team. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Priya Nair: Good thanks, Maya. Excited to see how this could replace some of our slow inference paths.
[00:12] Liam O'Connor: Awesome — we'll walk through a short live demo of hosted chat generation, then show the console recommendations in Optimize and talk about retries/backoff patterns.
[00:22] Sam Torres: Quick ask: we're very latency-sensitive for certain flows, and others can be batched. Hoping to hear concrete knobs.
[00:30] Liam O'Connor: Totally. We'll hit parameters like temperature, max_tokens, top_p, also streaming chunk sizes and suggested backoffs.

--- Demo start ---
[02:05] Liam O'Connor: Ok I'm sending a few live requests to the Redwood hosted chat endpoint. Note: streaming sends deltas as tokens are emitted, you can subscribe to partial events and render progressively.
[02:18] Elena Ruiz: Is the streamed content guaranteed order? We had a prior system that sometimes reordered chunks under retries.
[02:25] Liam O'Connor: Good question. Redwood ensures tokens are ordered per request. Retries are handled at the request boundary — if a retry is required we re-sent from the last confirmed byte, not reordering tokens. There are corner cases with network interruptions where the client needs to dedupe, so we recommend a client-side request id for idempotency.
[02:46] Maya Chen: We also expose a continuation token in case you want to resume a long-running chat if the connection drops.

[04:00] Sam Torres: How do you recommend we set retry/backoff? We had high rates of transient 502s with our previous provider.
[04:08] Liam O'Connor: Standard exponential backoff with jitter is what we recommend. For streaming, short-circuit retries for idempotent operations. Example: 100ms, 300ms, 1s, cap at 2s for the demo flows. For heavier throughput paths, combine with circuit breaker thresholds so you don't amplify load during infra blips.
[04:30] Priya Nair: Any idempotency token patterns you prefer?
[04:34] Liam O'Connor: Use a client-generated request_id header. For sync non-streaming generation, the server will dedupe duplicates within a short window. For streaming, you should treat partial receipts as best-effort and use resume tokens we return.

[06:12] Liam O'Connor: Now walking through parameters: temperature controls randomness — 0 to 1.2 typical range. Top_p is nucleus sampling. max_tokens limits output length. There's also stop sequences. For debug you can turn on logprobs.
[06:30] Elena Ruiz: Does Redwood support token-level warnings or cost estimation before generation?
[06:36] Maya Chen: In the Console you'll see token estimates per call and per-route cost breakdowns. Optimize will recommend larger batch sizes for non-latency critical routes to reduce per-token cost.

[07:50] Sam Torres: About batching — our batch windows are usually 50–200ms. Does Redwood's runtime maintain KV cache across requests to speed up short-turn convos?
[07:59] Liam O'Connor: Yes, we have prefix caching and KV cache for attention states. That reduces repeated compute for conversational turns, especially for pinned model versions. The cache is tenant-isolated in hosted.
[08:20] Priya Nair: What about data retention and logs? We need auditability for PHI flows.
[08:26] Maya Chen: For PHI you likely want Private deployment — but on hosted we can offer retention contracts and we have SOC 2 Type II. We can share the security pack after the call.

[09:15] Elena Ruiz: Could you show streaming error behavior — e.g., partial stream then socket close?
[09:20] Liam O'Connor: Sure — I'll simulate a socket drop.
[09:36] [sound of keyboard / pause]
[09:46] Liam O'Connor: Alright triggered a soft drop. You'll see the client got up to token 57, then connection closed. We surface a resume_token in the last event. If you reconnect and provide it, you can request the continuation instead of full regen — avoids drift.
[10:05] Sam Torres: That's useful. What happens if the model rolled while we were mid-stream?
[10:11] Liam O'Connor: We version models. If a model variant is rolled, the continuation fails safely and falls back to a short non-stream generation on the compatible version, then you can reconcile on the client. We log the change in the request trace.

[11:30] Maya Chen: Also highlight the console traces — you can see per-request latency histogram, token counts, and failure types. Liam — show Optimize's recommendation tab.
[11:40] Liam O'Connor: Pulling up Optimize — here we analyze your call patterns and suggest batching, quantization (if low-precision acceptable), and routing policies to cheaper model variants for non-critical paths. For example, we might suggest moving background summarization to a smaller model.
[12:10] Priya Nair: Do you provide automated A/B rollouts between variants?
[12:14] Liam O'Connor: Yep — rollouts and canary with automatic fallback. You can specify latency SLOs and if breached we fallback to the stable variant.

[13:40] Elena Ruiz: How do streaming connections authenticate? We use mTLS internally.
[13:45] Maya Chen: The hosted API uses token-based auth (Bearer), optionally combined with IP allowlists. For Private deployments you can integrate with your mTLS and VPC peering. We support SSO for the console and RBAC.

[15:00] Sam Torres: Performance question — what's typical cold-start on hosted? We've seen 2–3s elsewhere and that's too slow for some flows.
[15:07] Liam O'Connor: For short prompts on modern open models we often see sub-300ms first token on warm instances. Cold starts depend on queuing and model size; for strict low-latency we recommend pinned Dedicated pools. For hosted we do warm pools for high-traffic routes.

[17:20] Priya Nair: Cost wise, how do we balance latency pressure with token cost?
[17:26] Maya Chen: Two levers: use smaller model variants for non-critical flows and increase batching/prefetch for throughput workloads. Optimize will recommend batching thresholds and show unit economics per token. Also quantization profiles can cut inference cost at small quality tradeoffs.

[19:05] Liam O'Connor: Back to retries — when you get 429s we recommend client side rate limiting first, then exponential backoff. For 5xx errors, the typical policy is three retries with jitter and then escalate. For streaming, retry only whole requests or resume using the resume token if available.
[19:40] Elena Ruiz: Any SDKs that help with this built-in?
[19:44] Maya Chen: Our SDKs include idempotency helpers, retry policies, and streaming client helpers that surface resume tokens and partial events. We also publish language examples in the repo.

[21:10] Sam Torres: For observability, if we correlate request ids to our traces, is there a TTL on logs?
[21:16] Maya Chen: Hosted retains request-level traces for 90 days by default; enterprise retention can be extended. Audit logs are available for Private.

[23:00] Priya Nair: Security docs please — can you share SOC 2, data flow diagrams, and a summary of our options for PHI?
[23:08] Maya Chen: Absolutely. We'll attach the security pack and a short appendix on deployment choices.

[24:45] Liam O'Connor: Quick note on partial transcripts — sometimes auto-transcribe can mangle product names, so on the logs we use canonical model ids and version hashes.
[25:00] Elena Ruiz: That'll help.

[27:20] Maya Chen: Ok let's sketch a pilot: 2-week sandbox with keys, sample workload from Alder, and an SE-guided smoke test. After that, a POC check-in to review latency/cost and a security review with your compliance team.
[27:36] Priya Nair: Sounds good. Timeline: we'd like to run the sandbox this month and have a security call in two weeks.

[29:10] Sam Torres: One more question — competitors. We do parallel evals. Which similar vendors do you see us comparing you to?
[29:16] Maya Chen: Commonly mentioned are the big cloud managed endpoints, and a few inference infra vendors that offer self-hosted runtimes. We also see customers evaluating managed hosted LLM APIs.

[31:00] Elena Ruiz: For the resume token behavior — any edge cases where it might become invalid?
[31:06] Liam O'Connor: Resume tokens are short-lived (a few minutes) and tied to model variant; if you attempt to resume after a redeploy or model swap it will be rejected and you'll need to re-issue a full request.

[33:15] Maya Chen: Quick recap of next steps and docs we'll send. Liam — can you list the artifacts?
[33:20] Liam O'Connor: Sure — security pack (SOC2, DPA, data flow), SDK examples for retries and streaming, Optimize recommendation guide, and a sample pricing estimate for the pilot.

[34:10] Priya Nair: Please include the console walkthrough recording if possible.
[34:14] Maya Chen: Will do.

[35:00] Sam Torres: OK last: is there a way to surface per-token confidence or logprobs in the stream?
[35:07] Liam O'Connor: We can surface logprob deltas in the stream on request; that increases payload size and cost but useful for safety signals.

[36:40] Priya Nair: Thanks, this was helpful. We'll review internally and send a short list of sample prompts for the pilot.

[37:10] Maya Chen: Great — we'll follow up with the attachments and a pilot key. Thanks everyone.
[37:18] [meeting ends]
